extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and critical criteria for assessing and producing poetry, especially qualities exemplified in Wordsworth (style, imagery, imagination vs fancy) and principles of associative thinking used in poetic creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union of deep feeling with profound thought
rubrics_metrics.description: “It was the union of deep feeling with profound thought; the fine balance of truth in observing, with the imaginative faculty in modifying the objects observed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This union is presented as a chief merit: poetry should combine heartfelt emotion with intellectual depth. The critic praises work that balances truthful observation and imaginative enlargement rather than relying on sentiment or mere rhetorical flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent familiar objects so as to awaken a kindred feeling (freshness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “To represent familiar objects, as to awaken in the minds of others a kindred feeling concerning them, and that freshness of sensation…" (called the prime merit of genius).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should make common, familiar things appear fresh and emotionally stirring to readers—e.g., carrying childhood wonder into adult perception. Example invoked: new feeling on seeing snow after reading Burns. This is a core test of genius vs. mere talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance observation and imaginative modification
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fine balance of truth in observing, with the imaginative faculty in modifying the objects observed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetry observes accurately but allows imagination to modify perception to reveal meaning; excessive alteration or falsehood in observation undermines truth, while mere literal description lacks imaginative depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crowd or turbulence of imagery and forced diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Early faults: “crowd or turbulence of imagery; strained thought or forced diction” which justify complaints of obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overload a poem with competing images or use strained, artificial phrasing. Such excess demands undue close attention and creates obscurity. The critic favors clarity of association and economy of image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary, illogical, hackneyed, or fantastic phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: The text condemns “that worse defect of arbitrary and illogical phrases, at once hackneyed and fantastic,” common in ordinary poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction should avoid clichés and illogical phrase-making that call attention to themselves; the critic praises elimination of these defects as genius matures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language: strength without knotty contortion; avoid obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Language may be “peculiar and strong,” but when “knotty and contorted” it demands more attention than descriptive poetry ought to claim and can justify the complaint of obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet's language can be bold and novel, yet must not be so syntactically or lexically convoluted that it obstructs comprehension; stylistic novelty should not be a cover for incomprehensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manly reflection and human associations to enliven nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “Manly reflection and human associations had given both variety and an additional interest to natural objects.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems about nature should be infused with human thought and associative reflection to make scenes resonate; plain description without reflective associations is less compelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry childhood wonder into adult perception
rubrics_metrics.description: “To carry on the feelings of childhood into the powers of manhood; to combine the child's sense of wonder and novelty with the appearances which every day… had rendered familiar.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mark of genius is preserving the freshness and wonder of childhood viewpoint within mature poetic perception—this synthesis distinguishes genius from mere facility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware two opposing anti-patterns: seductive ornate faults and bald prosaic counterfeit
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasted faults: (a) “seductive faults… of Cowley, Marini, or Darwin” (ornate, corrupting taste) and (b) “a downright simpleness… prosaic words in feeble metre, silly thoughts in childish phrases, and a preference of mean, degrading, or at best trivial associations.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid both excessive ornate seduction that masks poor substance and the opposite extreme of banal, prosaic mimicry. Both can mislead public taste or create a spurious ‘school’ of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic choice: stanza form affects diction (Spenserian stanza caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Spenserian stanza… would doubtless have authorized… a more frequent descent to the phrases of ordinary life, than could… have been hazarded in the heroic couplet.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form influences allowable diction and tone; a poet should be aware that certain stanza forms license different levels of colloquial or ordinary phrasing without ill effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish imagination from fancy (two distinct faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author insists that “fancy and imagination were two distinct and widely different faculties,” proposing the term imagination for the higher faculty (Milton) and fancy for the lower (Cowley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical and creative precision requires recognizing these distinct functions: imagination (creative synthesis, high poetic power) vs. fancy (combinatory or decorative play). Using terms accurately guides evaluation and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Aristotelian law of association (five agents) in shaping thought and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle’s five agents of association: 1) connection in time (simultaneous, preceding or successive), 2) vicinity/connection in space, 3) interdependence/necessary connection (cause and effect), 4) likeness, and 5) contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are mechanisms by which parts of an impression recall others; poets may deliberately exploit temporal, spatial, causal, likeness, and contrast relations to craft associative chains and produce memorable imagery or transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association as mechanical memory vs imaginative synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: “In association then consists the whole mechanism of the reproduction of impressions… It is the universal law of the passive fancy and mechanical memory; that which supplies to all other faculties their objects.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the difference between passive associative recall (memory/fancy) and active imaginative synthesis; poets should use associative links purposefully but not confuse mere mechanical recall with creative imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of theoretical exposition: avoid needless obscurity in explaining poetics
rubrics_metrics.description: The author pledges to present an intelligible statement of his poetic creed and cites Hooker on the need to guard against 'complaints of obscurity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When articulating theory or craft, aim for perspicuity: readers should be given clear arguments and premises so criticism and instruction are useful rather than merely arcane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject reductionist mechanical hypotheses about mental association
rubrics_metrics.description: Hartley’s hypothetical vibrations and oscillating ether are criticized as untenable—reduction of association to mechanical propagation is deemed absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grounding poetic theory or explanation of creative processes in crude mechanical metaphors that cannot account for qualitative differences in ideas; prefer explanatory models that respect difference in mental content and creative synthesis.
